soil.title: Build Healthier Soil for Better Crops
soil.intro: Healthy soil is the foundation of a productive farm. It provides crops with nutrients, water, air and support throughout their growing cycle.
soil.whyTitle: Good crops start below the ground.
soil.whyDescription: Healthy soil helps roots access nutrients and water while supporting beneficial organisms. Understanding your soil before applying fertilizers can help reduce unnecessary input costs and improve crop management.
soil.guideDescription: Small improvements in soil management can make a difference over time. Focus on practices that match your crop, soil type and local conditions.

sections.title: Test Your Soil Before Fertilizing
sections.description: A soil test helps you understand pH and nutrient levels such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Use the results to guide fertilizer decisions instead of guessing.
sections.tip: Keep your latest soil-test report so you can compare changes over time.

sections.title: Give Crops the Nutrients They Need
sections.description: Different crops have different nutrient requirements. Apply fertilizers according to crop needs and soil-test recommendations.
sections.tip: More fertilizer does not always mean more yield.

sections.title: Return Organic Matter to the Soil
sections.description: Compost, farmyard manure and suitable crop residues can improve soil structure, moisture retention and biological activity.
sections.tip: Use well-decomposed organic material whenever possible.

sections.title: Rotate Crops Across Seasons
sections.description: Changing crops across seasons can help maintain nutrient balance and interrupt some pest and disease cycles.
sections.tip: Choose rotation crops according to your soil, climate and market.

sections.title: Protect Soil Structure
sections.description: Avoid unnecessary intensive tillage and protect exposed soil with suitable crop residues or mulch where appropriate.
sections.tip: Healthy soil structure supports better root growth and water movement.

doList: Test soil before making major fertilizer decisions.
avoidList: Do not apply fertilizer only because the crop looks weak.
Avoid leaving soil exposed to severe erosion.
Do not treat every field as if it has the same nutrient needs.
soil.farmerTip: Before spending more on fertilizers, understand what your soil actually needs. A soil test can turn guesswork into a more informed decision.
soil.takeaway: Healthy soil is not built in one season. Regular testing, balanced nutrition and good soil-management practices can protect productivity for years.

disease.title: Spot Crop Diseases Before They Spread
disease.intro: A small change in a leaf can sometimes be the first sign of a larger crop problem. Regular observation helps farmers notice unusual symptoms early and investigate them before the affected area becomes larger.
disease.whyTitle: Notice the warning signs before the problem grows.
disease.whyDescription: Crop diseases can spread through fields under suitable environmental conditions. Early observation gives farmers more time to identify the possible cause and choose an appropriate response.
disease.guideDescription: Regular monitoring, field hygiene and correct identification can help reduce avoidable crop losses.

sections.title: Walk Through the Field Regularly
sections.description: Inspect leaves, stems, flowers and fruits. Look at different parts of the field instead of checking only plants near the edge.
sections.tip: Pay closer attention after prolonged rain or humid conditions.

sections.title: Learn the Early Warning Signs
sections.description: Yellowing, spots, wilting, curling, discoloration or unusual growth can indicate a possible disease or another crop stress.
sections.tip: Take a clear photo when you first notice an unusual symptom.

sections.title: Check Before You Treat
sections.description: Not every yellow leaf or spot is caused by a disease. Nutrient deficiency, insects, weather and water stress can produce similar symptoms.
sections.tip: Correct identification should come before treatment.

sections.title: Remove Sources of Infection
sections.description: Where appropriate, remove severely affected plant material and manage infected crop residues according to local agricultural guidance.
sections.tip: Avoid spreading contaminated plant material around the field.

sections.title: Keep the Field Clean
sections.description: Manage weeds, remove unnecessary crop debris and avoid conditions that favour disease development.
sections.tip: Good field hygiene is part of crop protection.

doList: Consider weather conditions when assessing disease risk.
Ask a qualified agriculture expert when identification is uncertain.
avoidList: Do not assume every spot is a fungal disease.
Do not spray chemicals without identifying the problem.
Avoid using an old or unknown pesticide mixture.
Do not ignore disease symptoms until they spread.
Avoid moving infected plant material between fields.
disease.farmerTip: If you notice an unusual symptom, take a clear photo showing the whole plant and the affected part. This makes identification much easier.
disease.takeaway: Early observation does not guarantee that a crop disease can be prevented, but it gives farmers more time to identify the problem and respond appropriately.

water.title: Give Every Drop a Purpose
water.intro: Water is one of the most valuable resources on a farm. Good irrigation management is about giving crops the moisture they need while reducing unnecessary loss from evaporation, runoff and over-irrigation.

quickFacts.label: Focus irrigation where roots need it

water.whyTitle: The goal is not more water. It is better-timed water.
water.whyDescription: Too little water can stress crops, while unnecessary irrigation can waste water and create root or disease problems. Efficient irrigation depends on crop requirements, soil type, weather and the irrigation system available.
water.guideTitle: 5 ways to manage farm water better
water.guideDescription: Use these practical habits to make irrigation decisions based on crop and field conditions.

sections.title: Check the Weather First
sections.description: Consider recent rainfall and the short-term weather forecast before irrigating. Rainfall may reduce the immediate water requirement.
sections.tip: Use KrishiMitra's weather feature to check upcoming conditions.

sections.title: Irrigate According to the Crop
sections.description: Different crops and growth stages require different amounts of water. Avoid using the same irrigation schedule for every crop.
sections.tip: Crop stage matters when deciding irrigation needs.

sections.title: Check Soil Moisture
sections.description: Observe soil moisture around the root zone before watering. Irrigating when the soil is already sufficiently moist can waste water.
sections.tip: Check the soil rather than relying only on a fixed schedule.

sections.title: Use Efficient Irrigation
sections.description: Where suitable and affordable, systems such as drip irrigation can deliver water closer to plant roots and reduce some forms of water loss.
sections.tip: Choose an irrigation system based on crop, soil and farm conditions.

sections.title: Protect Moisture in the Soil
sections.description: Suitable mulching and crop-residue management can reduce evaporation from the soil surface and help maintain moisture.
sections.tip: Keep exposed soil protected where practical.

doList: Adjust irrigation according to crop stage.
avoidList: Do not irrigate automatically without checking field conditions.
Do not ignore leaking pipes or blocked emitters.
Avoid unnecessary flood irrigation where better options are suitable.
Do not treat every crop and soil type the same.
water.farmerTip: Before turning on the pump, check three things: recent rainfall, soil moisture and the crop's current growth stage.
water.takeaway: Efficient irrigation is about timing, quantity and observation. Give the crop what it needs while avoiding water that the soil and roots cannot use.
